hero.name: Ashwin
hero.who: a 34-year-old e-cycle founder in Coimbatore, brilliant but harsh, whose products confuse customers

story.b: Ashwin's company in Coimbatore makes electric cycles. He is talented, works eighteen-hour days and knows every bolt on every frame. But the company now sells nine different models, each with its own battery, charger and manual. Customers on the showroom floor look confused. Sales are flat. In meetings, Ashwin interrupts, dismisses ideas and once flung a prototype seat across the room. His team has stopped speaking up. One evening, a young delivery rider wheels a cycle back into the showroom. He cannot understand the display and wants a refund. Ashwin watches him leave and realises he has built many products, but not one that people truly love.

ask.q: Customers are confused and the team has gone quiet. What should Ashwin look at first?
o: Add more models so every customer finds something
Push the team to work longer hours to raise sales
Ask what customers would truly love, and how his behaviour affects the team
ask.why: More models deepen the confusion, and longer hours from a scared team rarely produce great work. Looking honestly at what customers really need, and at how his manner silences people, addresses the actual reasons the company is stuck.

chapters.take: Building many products is not the same as building one people love.

story.b: Ashwin covers a whiteboard with all nine models. Then he draws a simple grid: who rides, and why. Two needs stand out. College students who want a light, affordable cycle for short trips, and delivery riders who need a tough cycle with a long-lasting battery. He decides to make only two models and make them brilliant. Seven projects are cancelled, including a folding model he personally loved. The team is shocked, and a few are upset. But within weeks, engineers who were spread across nine products are working together on two. Battery problems that never got fixed are suddenly solved, because finally someone has time to focus on them.

ask.q: Ashwin's friend runs a bakery with forty items, many selling poorly. What does the idea suggest?
o: Focus on the few items people love most and drop the rest
Add new items each month to attract more customers
Keep all forty, since dropping items loses customers
ask.why: More items spread the bakers' effort even thinner, and keeping all forty protects the weak ones at the cost of the best. Saying no to good but ordinary items makes room to make a few excellent, which serves customers better.

chapters.take: Saying no to good ideas makes room for great ones.

story.b: The delivery rider's complaint stays with Ashwin. The display has seven buttons and a forty-page manual. His engineers suggest hiding the extra features in a menu. Ashwin says that only hides the mess. He spends weeks riding with delivery boys through Gandhipuram traffic, watching what they actually touch. Most of the time they need speed, battery left and lights. Nothing else. Making that work with one dial and one button takes far more effort than seven buttons ever did. The engineers rewrite the software three times. The manual shrinks to a single card. When a rider tries it, he figures it out in ten seconds and grins. That ease took Ashwin's team two months to build.

ask.q: Ashwin's team wants to keep all features but hide them in menus. What is the better approach?
o: Hide them, since it makes the screen look clean
Deeply understand what riders need and design only that, even if it takes longer
Add a longer manual so riders can learn everything
ask.why: Hiding features only moves the complexity somewhere else, and a longer manual asks riders to work harder. True simplicity comes from understanding the problem deeply enough to remove what is not needed. That takes real effort, but it makes the product easy.

chapters.take: Real simplicity is earned through hard, careful work.

story.b: The new cycle works well but looks like a machine part. Ashwin's sister, who teaches textile design, takes him to a handloom weaver near her college. Ashwin watches how colour, rhythm and touch make a simple cloth feel special. Back at work, he hires a young designer who studied fine arts, not engineering, and asks her to think about how the cycle feels. She changes the handlebar grip to a soft, cool material, picks two warm colours inspired by old Chettinad floor tiles and redesigns the bell to sound pleasant rather than harsh. The engineers call it fluff at first. Then test riders keep touching the grips and smiling. The cycle now feels human, not just useful.

ask.q: Ashwin's lead engineer says only specs matter, not colour or feel. How should Ashwin respond?
o: Bring together technical skill and a sense of people, art and feeling
Agree, since good engineering is enough on its own
Let the designer decide everything and ignore the engineers
ask.why: Pure specs can produce something that works but nobody loves, and ignoring engineers would make it beautiful but unreliable. Combining technical skill with an understanding of people, beauty and feeling creates products that feel human.

chapters.take: Great products need both technical skill and a feel for people.

story.b: Before launch, Ashwin buys his own product the way a customer would. Ordering on the website takes eleven steps on his phone. The cycle arrives in a box torn at one corner, and the charger comes in a separate parcel two days later. When he calls the service number with a made-up complaint, he waits twenty minutes. Each part was handled by a different team or vendor, and nobody owned the whole journey. So Ashwin gives one small team responsibility for everything, from the website to the first service visit. They cut ordering to three steps, redesign the box and pack the charger inside. At last, the experience matches the cycle.

ask.q: Ashwin's friend opens a café and focuses only on the coffee. What would the idea suggest?
o: Coffee is all that matters, so the rest can wait
Hire separate vendors for everything and let them decide
Think through the whole visit, from the menu and seating to the bill
ask.why: Great coffee in a cramped, slow, confusing café still leaves customers unhappy, and separate vendors make sure nobody owns the full visit. Thinking through every step, end to end, makes the whole experience feel cared for.

chapters.take: Customers judge the whole journey, not just your part of it.

story.b: During final testing, a brake sensor fails. Ashwin loses his temper in front of the whole team and calls the engineer, Meena, careless. She goes silent for days. Two others quietly start looking for jobs. Ashwin's sister tells him bluntly that his talent is real, but so is the damage he does. That night, Ashwin thinks about the best teacher he ever had, who was strict but never cruel. The next morning, he apologises to Meena privately. He tells her the sensor must be perfect and asks what she needs to get there. She fixes it in two days. Ashwin learns he can demand excellence and still treat people with respect.

ask.q: Ashwin's co-founder says harshness is the price of greatness. What is the better view?
o: Agree, since great products need a harsh leader
Keep high standards, give clear feedback privately and treat people with respect
Lower standards so nobody ever feels pressure
ask.why: Harshness may push some results, but it drives good people away and silences warnings. Lowering standards leads to ordinary products. Keeping the bar high while giving clear, respectful feedback gets the excellence without the damage.

chapters.take: You can demand excellence and still be kind.

story.b: Weeks later, the two new cycles launch in Coimbatore. On the first morning there is a line outside the showroom, mostly students and delivery riders. A rider tests the display, understands it in seconds and buys one on the spot. Customers keep running their hands over the grips. Every box arrives whole, with the charger inside. Meena now leads the brake team, and at the launch party she jokes with Ashwin without any fear. He still has high standards and still notices every flaw. But he says no more easily, listens longer in meetings and thanks people in public. Customers send photos of their cycles. Some have even given them names.

chapters.take: Focus, simplicity, care and respect together build products people love.
